extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants working on AI-related patent applications in Japan
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for patent examination of AI-related (CS/software) inventions before the Japan Patent Office, covering eligibility, description requirements, and inventive step with case examples. Intended to be used for drafting and examining AI/software patent applications in Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility — general criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the invention creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General criterion referenced to GL part III chap.1 and HB Annex B. (Mapped to Patent Law art.29(1) main paragraph.) This is the baseline test for whether subject-matter is an "invention."

rubrics_metrics.name: CS-related (software) eligibility — concrete realization
rubrics_metrics.description: Is information processing by the software concretely realized by using hardware resources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific criterion for CS-related inventions (HB Annex B). If information processing is concretely realized using hardware resources it is more likely to be considered a technical idea. JPO compares with US (Alice) two-step but applies Japan-specific approach; JPO described as more generous than the USPTO in some respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligible: mere presentation of information
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is only a mere presentation of information (e.g., sugar content data) is not a creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature and thus not an "invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Case 3-2): Claiming only data (sugar content data measured by a sensor) or data received/stored on a server without specifying means/method of presenting or concrete processing is not eligible. Claims must specify means or methods beyond mere information content/presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible: concrete information processing based on technical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim concretely performs information processing based on technical properties (e.g., chemical or biological properties) it can be a creation of a technical idea and thus eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Case 3-2 Claim 3): A prediction method that analyzes relationships between sugar content and meteorological conditions and predicts future sugar content—concrete processing using technical properties—was held eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement — clarity (claim-identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: One invention should be identified based on matters stated in one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapped to Patent Law art.36(6)(ii) and GL part III chap.2 sec.3. The description must support identification of the invention corresponding to each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement — support (scope-of-disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not the claimed invention exceeds 'the extent of disclosure in the description to which a person skilled in the art would recognize that a problem to be solved by the invention would be actually solved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapped to Patent Law art.36(6)(i). In AI cases, claims that go beyond the disclosed correlations, features, or training-data-supported relationships (e.g., claiming use of features not supported by description) fail the support requirement (Case 49 body weight estimation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement — enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not the description is clear and sufficient in such a manner as to enable any person ordinarily skilled in the art to work the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapped to Patent Law art.36(4)(i). For AI-related inventions, enablement requires sufficient disclosure (e.g., how models are generated, required data properties, processing steps) so a skilled person can reproduce the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-specific disclosure: training-data correlation/support requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlation among data in training data should be presumable in view of common general technical knowledge, or supported by an explanation or statistic information in the description, or supported by a performance evaluation of the AI model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit AI-focused requirement: if claimed relationships between inputs and outputs (features and labels) cannot be presumed from common general technical knowledge, the description must contain explanations/statistics or actual model performance evaluations to satisfy support/enablement. Failure to disclose correlations or performance evaluation can lead to lack of enablement/support (Case 46, Case 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step — general criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not it could be reasoned that a person skilled in the art easily arrives at the claimed invention based on the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapped to Patent Law art.29(2). The basic inventive-step inquiry is whether the claimed solution would have been obvious to a skilled person in view of cited prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for mixed-type (technical + non-technical) inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims mix technical and non-technical features, Japan does not distinguish between technical and non-technical features for inventive-step assessment, but features making no technical contribution cannot contribute to inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with EPO COMVIK approach; JPO will assess the whole claim but only technical contributions count toward inventive step. This affects AI/ software claims that include business or purely informational elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step: unexpected technical effect supports inventiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed feature that produces a significant technical effect that a person skilled in the art cannot expect can support a finding of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Case 34 Claim 2): Addition of temperature data led to a significant, non-obvious improvement (accounting for meltwater) and was held inventive. Emphasizes evaluating technical effect and whether it would be expected by the skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not inventive: mere systemization of human tasks using AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere systemization of tasks performed by humans by replacing them with AI (without technical contribution or unexpected technical effect) is not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Case 33 cancer level calculation apparatus): Using a trained neural network to perform a task that is well-known or is a direct systemization of existing human procedures was held not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting/format expectations (case-example driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should specify concrete means/methods and technical features rather than merely stating information content or abstract steps; one invention per claim and supported details are expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from multiple case examples: claims that lack means for concrete processing or that claim broad data items without technical implementation risk ineligibility or failure under description requirements. Use case examples in HB Annex A/B to guide appropriate claim scope and supporting disclosure.
